summary: This unit teaches you to inspect welded fabrications against their drawings, specifications and the WPS. You will plan inspections with an ITP and a weld map, inspect materials, fit-up and welding in progress, judge finished welds and sizes against written limits, understand the common NDT methods and carry out dye penetrant testing, and deal with rejected work through NCRs, repairs and clear, signed records.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It teaches you to carry out **basic inspection** of welded fabrications: planning the checks, inspecting steel and consumables when they arrive, checking fit-up before welding and the work while welding goes on, inspecting finished welds by eye and with gauges, checking sizes against the drawing, arranging simple non-destructive tests, and dealing with work that fails. You also learn to keep records that let every weld be traced.

At Level 3 you are no longer only checking your own welds. You check other people's work against written documents, and **your signature says the work meets them**. That is a real responsibility: judge against the written limits, not your own taste; measure, do not guess; and report what you find, including bad news.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders moving into leading-hand, supervisor or quality-control work in fabrication shops and on construction sites. You need the Level 2 knowledge of welding processes, joints and weld faults; this unit builds on it.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Read the drawing, the job specification, the welding procedure specification (WPS) and the code or procedure the job names; find the acceptance limits and tolerances; query anything that does not agree.
Write or follow an inspection and test plan (ITP) with hold and witness points; number every weld on a weld map; work out sample sizes.
Inspect safely with the right tools
Choose, check and use accurate gauges and measuring tools; control the hazards of the shop, the site and the test chemicals.
Check steel, certificates, consumables and gas on delivery; check welder qualifications; check fit-up and sign or refuse the hold point.
Check preheat, interpass temperature, settings against the WPS, cleaning between runs and the run sequence.
Inspect by eye, measure weld size and profile, name each fault and accept or reject it against the limits.
Measure lengths, positions, squareness, flatness and twist against the drawing tolerances.
Know what each common test can and cannot find; carry out dye penetrant testing; read test reports.
Mark, label and quarantine rejected work; write non-conformance reports (NCRs); see repairs re-inspected and closed.
Keep inspection records against weld numbers, write a short signed report, and report urgent problems at once.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, documents, goods-in, fit-up, in-process and visual inspection, weld faults, measurement, NDT, sampling, non-conformance, records and safety.

A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade terms) and essays, for example planning the inspection of a staircase, inspecting a delivery, the checks on a multi-run butt joint, judging faults, comparing NDT methods, dealing with a cracked weld, and keeping records with a weld map.

**Two group practicals**: a full inspection of a welded fabrication with planted faults (weld map, gauges, dimensions, dye penetrant, NCRs and a signed report); and goods-in, fit-up and in-process inspection with hold points signed or refused.

blocks.note: Short answers ask for exact terms such as leg length, throat, lack of fusion, overlap, arc strike, mill certificate, temperature crayon, interpass temperature, quarantine, witness point, magnifier, NDT and MPI. They are all in the key terms at the end.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Inspection, the documents and the plan

blocks.h: Why inspect, and why at stages

blocks.p: Inspection checks that the work matches what the client asked for, so that it is safe, fits, lasts and can be proved to meet the job's requirements. Inspecting **at stages** finds faults while they are still cheap and easy to put right. The later a fault is found, the more it costs.

head: When the fault is found
What putting it right involves
rows: Send the wrong or damaged steel back before anyone cuts it.
Re-set the joint: a few minutes with a grinder and clamps.
Grind out, re-weld and re-inspect: hours of work, and the extra heat may distort the job.
Strip the coating, repair the weld, then re-coat: days, and outside costs.
Travel, access equipment, crane hire, delay to the client, lost goodwill, and a risk that someone is hurt.

head: Document
What it tells the inspector
rows: Sizes and their tolerances (on each dimension or as a general tolerance in the title block), weld symbols (type, size, length and which side), materials and finish.
The client's requirements: which code or standard applies, which inspections and tests, how much NDT, what records, the coating.
The code or procedure the job names

The **acceptance limits** for weld faults (how deep an undercut may be, how big a pore), and the rules for qualifying welders and procedures. At the Centre this is the AWS code or procedure the Centre uses.
The process, joint design (bevel, root face, root gap), consumables, positions, current, voltage and travel speed ranges, preheat, interpass temperature and cleaning.
Which welder is approved for which process, position, material and thickness or diameter range, and whether the approval is still in date.
Every check, when it is done, how, against what, who does it and who signs.
Mill certificates for the steel and certificates for the consumables: their test results.
What was ordered and what has arrived.

blocks.p: **Acceptance criteria** (acceptance limits) say how big a fault may be before the weld is rejected. They come from the code or procedure named in the job specification, not from the inspector's opinion, the electrode packet or the welding machine's manual. Different jobs can have different limits: a garden gate may accept more than a lifting frame or a pressure pipe.
A **tolerance** says how far a size may be from the drawing size. 1500 ± 2 mm means any reading from 1498 mm to 1502 mm passes. 900 +0/−3 mm means 897 mm to 900 mm passes, and 901 mm fails.

blocks.note: If two documents disagree, for example the drawing shows a 6 mm fillet and the specification says 8 mm, do not choose one yourself. Raise a query with the person in charge (the engineer, supervisor or client's representative) and get the answer in writing before the work goes on.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: An **ITP** lists, in the order of the work, every inspection and test: the stage, what is checked, the method or tool, the document and limit it is checked against, who checks, who signs, and the record that proves it. It is agreed before work starts, often with the client.

head: Stage
What is checked, and how
Checked against
Point
rows: Steel sizes, condition, grade and heat numbers (tape, vernier, certificates); consumables and gas
Bevel, root face, root gap, alignment, cleanliness, tacks (gauges)
Preheat, settings, interpass temperature, cleaning between runs (crayons, clamp meter, eye)
Weld presence, size, profile and surface faults (gauges, light, mirror, magnifier)
Surface or internal faults (for example dye penetrant on 10% of welds)
Sizes, positions, squareness, flatness (tape, square, string line)
Every stage signed, NCRs closed, records complete

head: Type of point
What it means
Example
rows: Work **must stop** until the named person has inspected and signed off this stage.
No root run until the inspector has signed the fit-up.
The client (or their inspector) is told in good time and may come to watch. If they do not come at the agreed time, work may go on.
The client is invited to watch the dye penetrant testing.
Documents or records are checked, or the work is spot-checked, without stopping the work.
Mill certificates are reviewed and filed.

blocks.note: A hold point protects everyone. Once a root run is laid over a bad fit-up, the fault is hidden and costly to put right.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **weld map** is a copy of the drawing with every weld given a number (W1, W2, W3 …), usually in a logical order around the job. Each weld number then has its own line on the inspection record. The weld map lets you trace every weld: who welded it, with which WPS and electrode batch, what the inspection found, which NDT it had, and any NCR and repair. It is also how you choose and record NDT samples and how an NCR says exactly which weld failed.

sections.title: Safe inspection and the tools of the job

blocks.p: An inspector moves around a working shop or site, often close to welding, grinding and lifting. You must protect yourself and must not become a hazard to others.

head: Hazard
Where you meet it
How you control it
rows: Watching a welder to check settings and technique; passing open bays
Safety glasses with side shields at all times
A helmet or hand shield with the right filter shade whenever you look at the arc
Preheated joints, welds just made, parts in the sun
Treat all welded work as hot
Check with a temperature crayon, or wait
Eye protection, and a face shield near grinding
Dye penetrant cleaner, penetrant and developer aerosols; magnetic inks
Flammable: no arcs, sparks or smoking nearby
Gloves and eye protection as the safety data sheet (SDS) says
Inside tanks, vessels and box sections
Enter only with a permit, a gas test, ventilation and a standby person
Never use aerosols inside without the permit's controls
Turning heavy fabrications, cranes on site
Turn heavy parts with help or a hoist
Stay outside the barriers and signs until the radiographer says the area is clear
Cut edges, spatter, cables and offcuts
Look where you step; keep walkways clear

blocks.note: Never touch a weld to feel whether it is cool: steel that has stopped glowing looks the same hot or cold. Never look at an arc without a filter lens, even for a moment to check a setting.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Tool
Used for
Check before use
rows: Blade not kinked; end hook not bent or loose; calibration label in date
Plate and bar thickness, hole sizes
Reads zero with the jaws closed; jaws clean; battery
Straight edge, string line and spirit level
Straight edge not bent; level's bubble checked
Leg length and throat of fillet welds
Bevel angle, excess weld metal, fillet throat and leg, undercut and pit depth, misalignment
Misalignment (hi-lo) at the root of pipe and plate butt joints
Taper gauge, feeler gauges or gap gauges
Battery; set to the right range
Lighting the weld; seeing hidden sides and pipe roots; close looks at suspected cracks
Bright light; clean mirror and lens
Marking faults, weld numbers, rejects and quarantine

blocks.p: A reading is only as good as the tool that took it. Tools that give readings (tapes, calipers, gauges, thermometers, meters) are **calibrated**: checked against a known reference at set intervals, labelled with the date of the next check, and listed in a register. Between checks, look at each tool before you use it. Infrared thermometers read low on bright or shiny steel unless they are set for it; a contact thermometer or crayon is more reliable for preheat.

blocks.note: If a measuring tool is found damaged or reading wrong, take it out of use and label it, report it, and find which jobs it measured since its last good check. Those readings cannot be trusted, so the welds or sizes are measured again with a good tool. This is why inspection records note which tool was used.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Before welding: materials, consumables, welders and fit-up

flow: Check the delivery note against the purchase order: items, sizes, grades and quantities
Look at the condition: bends, dents, deep pitting, heavy rust, and laminations (layers) showing at cut edges
Measure: plate thickness with a vernier in several places, section sizes, lengths with a tape
Check the markings (grade and heat number) against the mill certificates
Accept: book it into the store, keep it off the ground, file the certificates in the job file
Reject or doubt: label it, move it to the quarantine area, record it, and tell the person in charge or the supplier

blocks.p: A **mill certificate** (mill test certificate) is the steel maker's record of the chemical analysis and strength test results for one **heat** (one batch melted together), identified by its **heat number**. Matching the heat number on the steel to the certificate gives **traceability**: if a problem appears later, the material can be traced to its test results, and other parts from the same heat can be found.

A shortage (fewer lengths than the delivery note says) is written on the delivery note and the goods-in record before anyone signs, and reported so it is chased. Never sign for goods that have not arrived.

blocks.note: When a length is cut, the end that carries the heat number may end up in the scrap bin. On traceable jobs, **transfer the heat number** to each piece with a paint marker or a low-stress stamp before it is cut, and record it on the cut list.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Steel for Jamaican jobs is mostly imported, and some arrives after weeks at sea or in an open yard. Look for heavy pitting and salt deposits, and do not accept substitute grades or sizes without written approval from the person in charge.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Item
What to check
rows: Type and size against the WPS (for example E7018, 3.2 mm)
Packet sealed, undamaged and dry; coating not cracked or chipped
Low-hydrogen electrodes into the holding oven once opened
Vacuum packs unbroken; once opened, used within the maker's exposure time or put in the oven
Type and diameter against the WPS; batch recorded
Spool sealed in its bag; no rust, kinks or dirt
The right gas: read the **label**, not only the colour (colours differ between suppliers and countries)
Cylinder within its test date; valve and regulator undamaged; stored upright and chained
Type and batch; kept clean and dry

blocks.p: Damaged or damp consumables are set aside, labelled and dealt with as the maker's data sheet says: re-dried if the maker allows it, otherwise rejected. Never guess a re-baking temperature.

Before a welder starts on work that must meet a code, check the **welder qualification record**. It shows the process, the position (for example 3G plate or 6G pipe), the material, the thickness and diameter range and the filler group the welder is approved for. Most codes also require **continuity**: the welder must have used that process within a set period (often six months), shown on a continuity log. A welder qualified on 1G plate is not approved for 6G pipe. Check too that the WPS itself is qualified, backed by a procedure qualification record (PQR).

head: Feature
What to check
Why it matters
Tool
rows: As the WPS says (a single-V is often 30–37.5° on each side)
Too small: lack of side-wall fusion and trapped slag. Too large: extra weld metal, heat and distortion
Too large: lack of root penetration. Too small: burn-through
As the WPS says, at several points along the joint
Too small: lack of penetration. Too large: burn-through, excess penetration, more weld metal
The step between the two surfaces at the root is within the limit
A step leaves one root edge unfused and raises stress
Joint and about 25 mm each side free of rust, scale, paint, oil and moisture
Right size and spacing; made to the WPS (with preheat if it asks) by a qualified welder; no cracks; ends ground to a taper (feathered)
A cracked tack passes its crack into the weld; a humped tack causes lack of fusion
Plates tight together; any gap within the limit
A gap makes the effective weld smaller; the code may require a bigger leg or a re-fit

blocks.p: Record the readings at the start, middle and end of each joint. Sign the hold point only when every reading is within the limits. If one is out, refuse the hold point, record the reading and the reason, have the joint re-fitted, and check it again.

blocks.note: Never sign a hold point you did not check yourself, and never sign it "to keep the job moving". Your signature is a statement of fact that others will rely on.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Some faults, such as hydrogen cracking, lack of fusion and trapped slag, cannot be seen once the weld is finished. In-process inspection checks that the WPS is being followed while the weld is made. You will not watch every run, but you check each welder and each joint type at the times the ITP sets.

head: Check
How
Why
rows: Temperature crayon or contact thermometer on the parent metal, at the distance from the joint the WPS gives (often about 75 mm), on both sides, before tacking and before each run
Slows cooling and lets hydrogen escape, preventing cracks in thick or hardenable steel
Measured just before the next run is laid
Too hot: lower strength and toughness and more distortion. Below the preheat: risk of cracking
Right electrode, wire and gas; electrodes taken from the oven or a heated quiver
Wrong or damp consumables cause weak or porous welds and cracks
Current, voltage, wire feed, gas flow
Machine display, clamp meter on the lead, flowmeter at the nozzle
They control heat input, fusion, penetration and bead shape
Time a measured length of run
Every run chipped and brushed, and looked at before the next
Slag left behind is trapped as an inclusion and causes lack of fusion
As the WPS or drawing says
Controls distortion and makes sure the root is sound
Screens in place for gas-shielded processes
Draughts blow away the shielding gas and cause porosity

ul: A **temperature crayon** leaves a mark that melts when the surface reaches the temperature printed on the crayon.
**Minimum preheat:** use a crayon rated at the minimum. If the mark melts, the steel has reached it.
**Maximum interpass:** use a crayon rated at the maximum. If the mark melts, the steel is too hot: wait until it has cooled below the limit before the next run.
Mark the parent metal beside the joint, not inside the bevel, so crayon residue cannot get into the weld.
Take the reading after the heating torch has been taken away for a moment, so you read the temperature through the steel and not just a hot surface.

blocks.p: Current, voltage and travel speed together set how much heat goes into the joint. Many WPSs give limits for it. The **arc energy** in kilojoules per millimetre is:

**Arc energy (kJ/mm) = (volts × amps × 60) ÷ (travel speed in mm/min × 1000)**. Some procedures multiply this by an efficiency factor for the process to give the heat input; use the method your WPS gives.

head: Step
Worked example: 22 V, 110 A, 150 mm of run laid in 75 seconds
rows: 150 mm in 75 s = 2 mm per second = 120 mm/min

blocks.p: More current or voltage, or slower travel, gives more heat input: a bigger, hotter weld, a wider heat-affected zone, more distortion and, on some steels, lower toughness. Too little heat input risks lack of fusion and a hard, crack-prone heat-affected zone. That is why a welder who "turns it up to get it done" is changing the weld, not just its speed.

blocks.note: Steel standing in the Jamaican sun can already be 50 °C or more, and the shop air is hot. That does not replace a WPS preheat, but it matters where the WPS sets a maximum interpass temperature, as on stainless steel. In the rainy season and on early mornings, joints may be wet with dew: they are dried (gently warmed) before welding. Sea breezes through open-sided shops blow away MIG and TIG shielding gas, so screens are needed.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: Write each reading down as you take it: time, joint, run, value and tool. A reading kept in your head is not a record.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Visual inspection and judging weld faults

ul: The welds are **cool**, and slag and spatter have been removed: they hide surface faults.

**Good light**: strong, even light (many standards ask for at least about 350 lux, and 500 lux is better). A torch held low across the surface throws shadows that show ripples, undercut and fine cracks.
Get close: your eye within about 600 mm of the surface, looking at an angle of not less than about 30° to it. Use a mirror for sides you cannot see and a magnifier for anything that might be a crack.
Have the weld map, the drawing, the acceptance limits, your gauges and the record sheet with you.

flow: Presence: every weld on the weld map is there, in the right place, at the right length
Size: leg lengths and throat on fillet welds; fill and reinforcement on butt welds
Profile: shape, convexity or concavity, and how smoothly the toes blend into the plate
Surface faults: cracks, undercut, porosity, overlap, incomplete fill, arc strikes, spatter, unfilled craters
Root, where you can see it: penetration, root concavity, burn-through
Compare every finding with the written limit
Mark rejects on the part, record every result against the weld number, decide accept or reject

blocks.p: Fillet weld size is usually given as the **leg length**: the distance from the root of the joint to the toe, along the face of each plate. Some drawings give the **throat** instead: the shortest distance from the root to the face of the weld. On an equal-leg fillet with a flat face between plates at 90°, the throat is about **0.7 × the leg length**.

ul: **Convex** fillet: the extra metal on the face adds no strength. The throat that counts is measured to a straight line between the toes.
**Concave** fillet: the legs can be full size while the throat is too small. Measure the throat as well as the legs.
**Unequal legs**: measure both legs; each must meet the drawing.
An **undersize** weld may not carry its load. An **oversize** weld wastes metal and time, adds heat and distortion, and does not make up for a poor joint.

blocks.p: A butt weld should be filled flush with the plate surface or a little above it. **Excess weld metal** (too much cap height or reinforcement) is a fault, not a bonus: the sharp angle at the toes concentrates stress and shortens the weld's life under changing loads, and it wastes filler and grinding time. **Incomplete fill** (underfill) leaves the face below the plate surface, so the weld is too thin. At the root, look for **lack of root penetration**, **excess penetration**, **root concavity** (the root bead sucked back into the joint) and **burn-through**. Pipe roots you cannot see directly are checked with a mirror and torch or a borescope.

blocks.h: Common faults and how to judge them

head: Fault
What you see
Likely causes
How it is found
Usual decision
rows: A line in the weld or the heat-affected zone; star-shaped in an unfilled crater
No preheat on thick steel; fast cooling
Eye and magnifier; dye penetrant or magnetic particle to find its ends; ultrasonic or radiography inside
Rejected at any size in almost every code
A groove melted into the plate along the toe and left unfilled
Travel too fast; no pause at the edges of a weave
Eye; depth measured with an undercut or bridge cam gauge
Accepted only up to the depth (and length) the limits allow
Round gas holes, alone, in clusters or in a line
Rust, oil, paint or zinc on the joint
Loss of shielding gas: draught, leak, wrong flow, blocked nozzle
Surface pores by eye; buried pores by radiography
Limited in size and number by the code; some jobs accept none
Weld metal rolled onto the plate at the toe without fusing
Eye; the tip of a gauge catches under it
Weld metal not melted into the side wall or the run below; sometimes a line at the toe
Slag or mill scale left on the joint
Often hidden: ultrasonic testing or a bend test; sometimes seen at the surface
Gap too small or root face too big
Current too low or electrode too big
From the root side by eye, mirror or borescope; radiography
Face below the plate surface; fillet short of size
Too few runs or runs too small
Cap or fillet face too high
A small burnt spot on the plate away from the weld
Holder or clamp touching the work
Usually ground smooth and checked for cracks as the procedure says
Small balls of metal stuck around the weld
Slag trapped in the face or between runs

blocks.p: For each finding: **name** it, **measure** it, **compare** it with the written limit, **decide** accept or reject, and **record** it against the weld number. If you are not sure whether a line is a crack, treat it as a crack until a magnifier, dye penetrant or magnetic particle test shows otherwise.

blocks.note: Judge against the written limits. A rough-looking weld may be within the limits; a neat-looking weld can still be undersize or cracked. Record measurements, not opinions.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: When one welder keeps producing the same fault, for example undercut on vertical welds, do not just keep rejecting the welds. Show the welder the fault and the measurements, explain the likely cause (often too much current, or no pause at the edges of the weave), watch the next test piece, and check the next production welds. Record what you did, and tell the supervisor if retraining or a retest is needed.
A fabrication can have perfect welds and still be useless if it does not fit. Dimensional inspection checks the finished job against the drawing.

flow: Wait until the job is cool, and set it on level trestles or stands so its own weight does not bend or twist it
From the drawing, list the key sizes, their tolerances (on the dimension or the general tolerance in the title block) and the datum the sizes are measured from
Measure the overall length, width and height
Measure the positions of holes, brackets and cleats from the datum, and the hole sizes and spacings
Check squareness by measuring both diagonals
Check flatness and straightness with a string line or straight edge, and twist on level supports
Write each reading beside the drawing size with pass or fail and the tool used; mark and raise an NCR for anything out of tolerance

blocks.p: In a true rectangle both diagonals are equal. The diagonal length comes from Pythagoras: **diagonal = √(length² + width²)**. For a frame 1600 mm × 1200 mm: 1600² + 1200² = 2 560 000 + 1 440 000 = 4 000 000, and √4 000 000 = **2000 mm**. Measure both diagonals from the same points on each corner (for example the outside corners, or centre-punch marks) and compare the **difference** between them with the limit on the drawing or in the procedure.
Equal diagonals show the frame is square, not that its sizes are right: a frame can be square and still too long. Check both.

ul: **String line**: stretch a line over two blocks of the same height at each end of a member, and measure the gap from the line to the steel at intervals.
**Straight edge and feeler gauges**: lay the straight edge on the surface and measure any gap under it.

**Twist**: on level supports, a twisted frame rocks on two opposite corners; measure the gap under the corner that lifts. You can also sight across two straight edges laid across each end: if they are not parallel, the frame is twisted.

blocks.note: A long member in the midday sun can be much hotter than your tape. Steel grows about 0.0115 mm per metre for every 1 °C, so a 6 m member 25 °C hotter than the tape is about 1.7 mm longer. For close tolerances, measure in the shade or at a cooler time, with tape and steel at the same temperature.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: The dimensional record lists each check, the drawing size and tolerance, the actual reading, pass or fail, the tool used (with its number), and the inspector's name, signature and date. Anything out of tolerance is marked on the part and raised as a non-conformance.

**Non-destructive testing (NDT)** checks welds without damaging them. Visual inspection is the first NDT method and always comes first. The other methods are carried out and interpreted by **technicians qualified and certified in that method**. As a Level 3 inspector you must know what each one can and cannot find, so you can plan it, prepare the work, keep the area safe and read the reports. You will carry out dye penetrant testing yourself in training.

head: Method
How it works
What it finds
Limits
rows: Surface faults, weld size and profile
A red or fluorescent liquid soaks into openings in the surface; a white developer draws it back out to show them
Cracks, pores and laps that break the surface, on any non-porous metal, including stainless steel and aluminium
Surface-breaking faults only; needs a clean, dry surface within the kit's temperature range
The part is magnetised (often with a yoke); fine iron particles gather where a crack disturbs the magnetic field
Cracks at the surface and just below it, quickly, on magnetic steels
Magnetic materials only, so not austenitic stainless steel or aluminium; test in two directions at right angles
A probe sends high-frequency sound into the weld; echoes from faults show on a screen
Hidden faults such as lack of fusion, cracks and lack of penetration, with their depth and position; needs access from one side only
Needs a qualified operator and a couplant gel; difficult on thin, rough or awkward shapes
X-rays or gamma rays pass through the weld onto film or a digital plate
Porosity, slag, lack of penetration and some cracks; gives a permanent picture
Radiation hazard (controlled area); needs access to both sides; slow and costly; can miss flat faults lying across the beam

blocks.h: Dye penetrant testing, step by step

flow: Read the SDS; put on gloves and eye protection; make sure there is ventilation and no arc, flame or spark nearby; check the part is within the kit's temperature range
Pre-clean: remove slag, spatter, paint and oil with the cleaner; let the surface dry
Apply the penetrant over the area and leave it for the dwell time the maker gives (often 10–30 minutes); do not let it dry out
Remove the excess: wipe with a dry, lint-free cloth, then with a cloth lightly dampened with cleaner. Do not spray cleaner straight onto the area: it washes penetrant out of the faults
Shake the developer can well and spray a thin, even white coat from the distance the maker gives
After the development time the maker gives (often about 10 minutes), inspect in good light: red lines show cracks, red dots show pores
Record the weld number, the position and length of each indication (a photo helps), then clean the part

blocks.note: Steel in the midday sun can be well over 50 °C, hotter than many penetrant kits allow (check the can), and the penetrant dries in the faults. Test in the shade, early in the day, or after the part has cooled.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Some tests destroy the piece and so are used on test pieces, not on the job: welder and procedure qualification tests and production test plates. A **bend test** opens up lack of fusion; a **macro-etch** (a cut, polished and etched section) shows penetration, fusion and the run layout; **nick-break** and **fillet-break** tests snap the weld so you can see inside it; a **tensile test** measures strength.
Visual inspection is usually 100%: every weld. NDT is often done on a **sample**, a percentage the ITP or specification sets. Work out the number, and always round **up** to a whole weld.

ul: Choose the sample fairly: welds from every welder, every position and every part of the job, plus any weld that looks doubtful.

If welds in the sample fail, the ITP or code says what happens next. Commonly more welds by the same welder or of the same type are tested; if those fail too, all of them are tested. Always look for the cause as well.
Check every NDT report: weld number, method, result, the position of any indication, the operator's qualification and the date. Rejected welds go onto NCRs.

flow: Mark the fault on the part with a paint marker, with the weld number
Label the part REJECT or HOLD and move it to the quarantine area if it can be moved
Stop further work on it: no painting, galvanising, shipping or lifting
Write a non-conformance report (NCR) and report it to the person in charge
The person with authority decides what will be done (the disposition)
Find the cause and check similar work
Repair to an approved method, then re-inspect to the same standard
Record the result, sign the NCR as closed and remove the label

head: The NCR records
Example
rows: Weld W17 on the weld map, 120 mm from the north end
Undercut 1.2 mm deep, 60 mm long, upper toe
The requirement it does not meet
Job limit 0.5 mm (the code or procedure named in the specification)
Repair: grind and re-weld to WPS-07
Current above the WPS range; welder briefed, settings checked daily

head: Disposition
What it means
Who decides
rows: Bring the work up to the requirement by an approved repair
Inspector and supervisor, to the approved method
Re-make the part, or re-fit and re-weld
Accept the work as it is, although it does not meet the requirement
Only the person with authority (the engineer or client), **in writing**

ul: Remove the fault completely, by grinding or gouging, back to sound metal.
For a crack, find its ends first with dye penetrant or magnetic particle, and check again after grinding that it has all gone.
Re-weld to the WPS or an approved repair procedure, by a qualified welder, with any preheat it needs.
Re-inspect to the same standard, with the same NDT (or more, if the specification says).
Many specifications limit how often one spot may be repaired. Check before a second repair.

blocks.p: A repair fixes one weld; finding the cause stops the next one. Look at other welds by the same welder, from the same electrode batch, on the same shift or in the same position. Cracks in several welds made with E7018 from a box left open on the bench point to the electrode storage, not to the welder alone.

head: Poor entry
Useful entry
rows: "W1–W12: 100% visual; legs 8–9 mm (8 mm required); no faults; accept. 14 Oct 2026, T. Brown, gauge FG-03."
"W7: undercut 1.0 mm deep × 40 mm at upper toe; limit 0.5 mm; reject, NCR-012."
"Frame F2: diagonals 2000 and 2002 mm; limit 3 mm difference; accept. Tape T-05."

blocks.p: The full set of records goes in the **job file** (sometimes called a data book): the weld map, goods-in and certificates, welder approvals, fit-up and in-process records, visual and dimensional records, NDT reports, NCRs and the final release. Each record is signed and dated.

Before an item leaves the shop, the final inspection confirms that every stage on the ITP has been done and signed, every NCR is closed, all NDT reports are in, the sizes have been checked, and the records are complete. If anything is missing, the item is not released.

The inspection report is short and factual: the job, the scope, what was inspected and how, the numbers of welds inspected, rejected and repaired, anything not inspected and why, any open NCRs, the overall result, and your signature and date. Anything that puts people at risk is reported **at once**, by word of mouth and then in writing. A crack in a lifting lug on a frame due to be lifted today means the lift stops until it is dealt with.

blocks.note: Never sign for a check you did not do, never change a reading because someone is in a hurry, and report the true results even when they are unwelcome. Inspection records may be read years later, after a failure or in court.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain why inspection is done at stages, and what a fault costs when it is found late.
I can name the documents I inspect against and find the acceptance limits and tolerances in them.
I can raise a query when two documents disagree, instead of choosing one myself.
I can read and help write an ITP, and explain hold, witness and review points.
I can draw a weld map and use weld numbers on every record.
I can control the hazards of inspection work, including arc light, hot metal, test chemicals, confined spaces, height and radiography.
I can choose, check and use measuring tools and gauges, and say what to do when one is found inaccurate.
I can inspect a delivery of steel and consumables, match heat numbers to mill certificates and quarantine anything that fails.
I can check a welder's qualification range and continuity.
I can inspect a fit-up and decide whether to sign the hold point.
I can check preheat and interpass temperatures with crayons, and settings against the WPS, and work out arc energy.
I can carry out a visual inspection, measure leg length and throat, and name the common weld faults with their causes.
I can accept or reject a weld against written limits and record the result.
I can check sizes, squareness, flatness and twist against drawing tolerances.
I can say what visual, dye penetrant, magnetic particle, ultrasonic and radiographic testing can and cannot find.
I can carry out dye penetrant testing in the right steps.
I can work out a sample size and a failure rate.
I can mark, label and quarantine rejects, write an NCR and see a repair through to close-out.
I can write clear inspection records and a short signed report.
I can report an urgent safety problem at once and stop the work it affects.

terms: Acceptance criteria
The written limits that say how big a fault may be before the work is rejected
Arc energy
Heat put in by the arc per millimetre of weld: volts × amps × 60 ÷ (travel speed in mm/min × 1000), in kJ/mm
Arc strike
A burnt mark on the plate away from the weld where an arc was struck by mistake
Calibration
Checking a measuring tool against a known reference at set intervals
Concession
Written permission from the person with authority to use work that does not meet the requirement
Continuity
Proof that a qualified welder has kept using the process within the period the code sets
Dye penetrant (PT)
An NDT method that shows surface-breaking faults with a coloured liquid and a developer
Excess weld metal
Weld metal standing too far above the plate surface on a butt weld
Fit-up
How the parts are set up and tacked before welding: gap, bevel, root face and alignment
Heat number
The number that identifies one batch (heat) of steel and links it to its mill certificate
Hi-lo
Misalignment: one surface standing higher than the other at the root of a butt joint
Hold point
A stage where work must stop until the named person has inspected and signed it off
Inspection and test plan (ITP)
The list of every check and test on a job: when, how, against what, by whom and who signs
Interpass temperature
The temperature of the weld area just before the next run is laid
Lack of fusion
Weld metal not melted into the parent metal or into the run below
Leg length
The distance from the root of a fillet weld to its toe, along the face of the plate
Magnetic particle inspection (MPI)
An NDT method that shows surface and near-surface cracks in magnetic steel with iron particles
Magnifier
A hand lens used to look closely at a weld surface for fine cracks
Mill certificate
The steel maker's document giving the chemical and strength test results for a heat of steel
Non-conformance report (NCR)
The record of work that does not meet its requirement, and of what is done about it
Non-destructive testing (NDT)
Testing a weld without damaging it
Overlap
Weld metal spilled onto the plate at the toe without fusing to it
Preheat
Heating the parent metal before welding to the temperature the WPS gives
Quarantine area
A marked area where rejected or doubtful material is kept so it cannot be used by mistake
Radiography (RT)
An NDT method that makes a picture of the inside of a weld with X-rays or gamma rays
Temperature crayon
A marker that melts at a set temperature, used to check preheat and interpass temperature
Throat
The shortest distance from the root of a fillet weld to its face; about 0.7 × the leg on an equal-leg, flat-faced fillet
Tolerance
How far a size may differ from the drawing size and still pass
Traceability
Being able to follow a part or weld back to its materials, welder, procedure and test results
Ultrasonic testing (UT)
An NDT method that finds hidden faults with high-frequency sound
Undercut
A groove melted into the parent metal at the toe and left unfilled
Weld map
A drawing with every weld numbered, used to record and trace each one
Witness point
A stage the client is invited to watch; work may go on if they do not come
WPS
Welding procedure specification: the approved method for making a weld

c1.title: Goods-in for church-hall trusses in Falmouth
c1.text: Kerry-Ann is the Level 3 inspector at a fabrication shop in Falmouth, Trelawny, which is making roof trusses for a church hall. A delivery arrives: 65 × 65 × 6 mm angle, 12 mm gusset plate and 3.2 mm E7018 electrodes. The delivery note lists 24 lengths of angle; she counts 22. The heat number painted on one bundle of angle does not appear on any of the mill certificates that came with the load. One carton of E7018 is a sealed vacuum pack with no damage. The job specification asks for every truss member to be traceable to its certificate.

c2.title: Pipe spools for a pumping station in Lionel Town
c2.text: Damion inspects carbon steel pipe spools at a shop in Lionel Town, Clarendon, for a water-pumping station. The WPS for the butt welds gives: root gap 2.5–3.5 mm, maximum misalignment 1.5 mm, minimum preheat 80 °C, maximum interpass temperature 250 °C, and 3.2 mm E7018 fill runs at 100–130 A. On joint J4 the root gap measures 3.0 mm at two points and 2.0 mm at a third, and the misalignment is 2.5 mm. The welder, Shane, holds a current 6G pipe qualification for this process.

c3.title: A tank platform in Ocho Rios
c3.text: Shanice inspects the fillet welds on a steel platform that will carry water tanks at a hotel in Ocho Rios, St Ann. The drawing calls for 8 mm fillets. The job's limits say: no cracks; undercut no deeper than 0.5 mm; a fillet may be up to 1 mm under size, but only over 10% of its length. Weld W14 has 8 mm legs but a strongly hollow (concave) face. W22 has undercut measured at 0.3 mm deep. W31 has a small star-shaped crack in the crater at its end. W9 measures 6.5 mm on both legs along its whole 300 mm length.

c4.title: School gate frames in Morant Bay
c4.text: Jermaine checks six welded gate frames for a school at a shop in Morant Bay, St Thomas, before they go for painting. The drawing gives each frame as 2400 mm × 1000 mm, with ± 2 mm on length and width, and says the two diagonals must be within 3 mm of each other. The frames are lying on rough, uneven ground in the yard. Frame 4 measures 2401 mm × 999 mm, and its diagonals are 2598 mm and 2605 mm.

c5.title: Conveyor brackets in Bog Walk
c5.text: Tricia leads inspection at a shop in Bog Walk, St Catherine, on 120 identical brackets for a factory conveyor. Each bracket has two fillet welds. The ITP asks for 100% visual inspection and magnetic particle testing of 5% of the welds. One bracket has a bolt hole drilled 3 mm out of position, outside the drawing tolerance, and the factory wants the brackets urgently. At the end of the job Tricia must write the inspection report.

questions.q: What should Kerry-Ann do with the bundle of angle whose heat number is on none of the certificates?
o: Use it for the purlins, which carry less load than the trusses
Keep it labelled in quarantine until a matching certificate comes
Accept it, since all angle of this size is made to the same steel grade
Paint a heat number from one of the certificates onto the bundle
questions.why: Steel that cannot be matched to a certificate cannot be traced to its test results, and this job asks for traceability. It is kept apart and labelled until the supplier provides the right certificate or it is rejected.

questions.q: How should she deal with the two lengths of angle that did not arrive?
o: Sign for all 24 lengths, as the driver says the rest will come next week
Send the whole load back until the two missing lengths can be delivered
Shorten the cut list so the 22 lengths will cover all of the trusses
Write the shortage on the delivery note and record, then report it
questions.why: Signing for goods that have not arrived makes the record false and loses the claim on the supplier. Writing the shortage on the delivery note before signing, and reporting it, gets it chased.

questions.q: What is the right way to store the sealed vacuum pack of E7018?
o: Open it now and bake the electrodes, so they are ready when needed
Open it to check the electrodes are dry, then tape the pack shut again
Keep it sealed until needed, then follow the maker's time limit
Put it straight into the holding oven at once, still in its sealed pack
questions.why: An undamaged vacuum pack keeps low-hydrogen electrodes dry, so it stays sealed until needed. Once it is opened the maker gives a time within which they must be used, or they go into the holding oven.

questions.q: The fabricator will cut the angle into truss members. How is traceability kept?
o: The heat number is written on the cut list once all the cutting is done
The heat number is moved onto each piece before the length is cut
Each truss gets a number painted on it after the welding is finished
The mill certificates are pinned to the wall beside the cutting saw
questions.why: The marked end of a length may become scrap, so the heat number is transferred to every piece before cutting and recorded on the cut list. Each member can then be traced to its certificate.

questions.q: What should Damion do at the fit-up hold point for joint J4?
o: Sign it, as two of the three gap readings are inside the WPS range
Sign it, and let Shane use more current to get through the tight gap
Sign it, but write the low reading and misalignment in the final report
Refuse to sign, record the readings, and have the joint re-fitted
questions.why: The 2.0 mm gap and the 2.5 mm misalignment are both outside the WPS limits, and both lead to lack of root penetration. The hold point is refused and recorded, and the joint is re-fitted and checked again.

questions.q: How should Damion use temperature crayons to check the preheat before the root run?
o: Mark inside the bevel with a 250 °C crayon and check that it does not melt
Mark the joint after the root run with an 80 °C crayon to see it stayed hot
Mark the steel beside the joint with an 80 °C crayon; it should melt
Hold an 80 °C crayon in the heating flame until the crayon starts to melt
questions.why: A crayon melts when the steel reaches its rating, so an 80 °C mark that melts shows the minimum preheat has been reached. Mark the parent metal beside the joint, not inside the bevel, and test before welding.

questions.q: Between two fill runs, Damion's 250 °C crayon mark melts as soon as it touches the pipe. What should happen?
o: Welding carries on, as the joint is well above its minimum preheat
Shane lets it cool below 250 °C before he lays the next run
Shane turns the current up so the next run keeps the heat even
The joint is cooled quickly with a wet rag to save waiting time
questions.why: A 250 °C crayon that melts shows the joint is above the maximum interpass temperature. The next run waits until it has cooled in air below the limit; quenching with water can crack the weld.

questions.q: A clamp meter shows 145 A while Shane lays a fill run. What should Damion do?
o: Stop the welding, have the current corrected, and record it
Accept it, since a higher current only gives the weld better fusion
Note it for the final report and let Shane finish this joint first
Ask Shane to travel faster so that the heat input stays about the same
questions.why: 145 A is outside the WPS range of 100–130 A, and the WPS is the approved method. Damion stops the work, gets the setting corrected, records it, and reports it so the weld already made can be judged.

questions.q: W14 has 8 mm legs but a strongly concave face. Why might it still fail?
o: Its legs are 8 mm, so its throat must also be the full size
A concave face is always a sign of cracking under the surface
A concave face can only be accepted on welds in the flat position
Its throat may be well short of the 5.6 mm it needs
questions.why: On a flat-faced 8 mm fillet the throat is about 0.7 × 8 = 5.6 mm. A hollow face can leave the throat much smaller even when the legs are full size, so the throat is measured too.

questions.q: What should Shanice decide about the undercut on W22?
o: Reject it, because any undercut at all weakens the weld at its toe
Accept it and record the depth she measured against the weld number
Send it for radiography to find out how deep the undercut really goes
Have it ground smooth, as the client will expect a perfect finish
questions.why: 0.3 mm is within the job's 0.5 mm limit, so the weld is accepted. Inspectors judge against the written limits, and the measured depth is recorded so the decision can be checked later.

questions.q: W31 is rejected for its crater crack. How should the repair be checked before it is accepted?
o: Grind it out, prove it gone with dye penetrant, re-weld, re-inspect
Weld a second run over the crater so that the crack is covered and sealed
Fill the crack with a small run and check that the new surface looks smooth
Grind the surface smooth, since a crater crack is only on the surface
questions.why: A crack covered by a new run is still there and can grow. It is removed to sound metal, a surface test confirms it has gone, and the repair is welded and then re-inspected to the same standard.

questions.q: What is the correct decision for W9?
o: Accept it, because 6.5 mm is close enough to the 8 mm on the drawing
Accept it, because it is under size by less than 2 mm on each leg
Reject it: it is 1.5 mm under size along its whole length
Reject it only if a dye penetrant test also shows a fault in it
questions.why: The limit allows at most 1 mm under size over 10% of the length. W9 is 1.5 mm short along all 300 mm, so it fails and is recorded for repair, as an undersize weld may not carry its load.

questions.q: What should the two diagonals be on a frame that is exactly 2400 mm × 1000 mm?
questions.why: By Pythagoras, √(2400² + 1000²) = √(5 760 000 + 1 000 000) = √6 760 000 = 2600 mm. Adding the two sides (3400 mm) is a common mistake.

questions.q: What should Jermaine record for frame 4?
o: Pass: each diagonal is within 5 mm of the 2600 mm it should measure
Fail on length, because 2401 mm is longer than the size on the drawing
Sizes pass, but it is out of square: the diagonals are 7 mm apart
Pass, because the average of the two diagonals is close to 2600 mm
questions.why: Length and width are within ± 2 mm, but the diagonals differ by 2605 − 2598 = 7 mm, more than the 3 mm allowed, so the frame is out of square. It is recorded and raised as a non-conformance.

questions.q: Why should Jermaine move the frames before checking them for flatness and twist?
o: Uneven ground can twist a frame, so readings would be false
Frames lying on the ground are too awkward to reach for measuring
Steel on the ground is cooler, which makes the tape measure read short
The school's inspector will want to see frames standing up on trestles
questions.why: A frame resting on uneven ground takes up the shape of its supports. Set it on level trestles so that its own shape, not the ground's, is measured.

questions.q: How many welds must be given magnetic particle testing?
questions.why: The sample is 5% of the welds, not of the brackets: 120 brackets × 2 welds = 240 welds, and 240 × 5 ÷ 100 = 12. Taking 5% of the 120 brackets gives the wrong figure of 6.

questions.q: Who may decide that the bracket with the misplaced hole can be used as it is?
o: Tricia, if she judges that the bracket will still bolt up
The welder who drilled it, if he signs to say the bracket is fine
The client's engineer, or another with authority, in writing
The shop foreman, because the factory needs the brackets urgently
questions.why: Using non-conforming work as it is is a concession. Only someone with authority over the design or contract can grant it, in writing on the NCR; urgency does not change that.

questions.q: Which item must Tricia's inspection report include?
o: The names of the welders who were slowest at finishing their brackets
Her own view of whether the drawing's tolerances were too strict
A copy of the factory's order with its agreed price for the brackets
The numbers inspected, rejected and repaired, and any not checked
questions.why: A report gives the scope and the results: what was inspected, how much failed, what was repaired, anything left uninspected, open NCRs and the overall result, signed and dated.

questions.q: Which test would best find lack of side-wall fusion buried in the middle of a 20 mm thick butt weld?
o: Dye penetrant testing
Ultrasonic testing
Visual inspection with a magnifier
Magnetic particle testing
questions.why: Lack of fusion deep inside a thick weld does not reach the surface, so visual, dye penetrant and magnetic particle methods cannot find it. Ultrasonic sound reflects from it and shows its depth.

questions.q: A welder runs at 24 V and 140 A, with a travel speed of 160 mm/min. What is the arc energy?
o: About 1.26 kJ/mm
About 0.53 kJ/mm
About 2.10 kJ/mm
About 12.6 kJ/mm
questions.why: Arc energy = 24 × 140 × 60 ÷ (160 × 1000) = 201 600 ÷ 160 000 = about 1.26 kJ/mm. Check the units: a slip with the 60 or the 1000 gives an answer many times too big or too small.
